stories.headline: IRAN STRIKES TWO OIL TANKERS IN THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ, PUSHING WTI CRUDE PAST $86 AND UP MORE THAN 20% FOR THE MONTH
stories.body: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said Friday it struck two tankers operating under U.S. military escort as they tried to transit the Strait of Hormuz, forcing four other vessels to reverse course; WTI crude jumped about 3.5% to $86.80 a barrel, extending July's gain past 20% as traders price in disruption risk to a route carrying roughly a quarter of the world's seaborne oil.
stories.explain: The Strait of Hormuz is the only maritime exit from the Persian Gulf, so a credible threat to tanker traffic forces oil prices to move immediately on the risk of disrupted supply, well before any barrels actually stop flowing, because shippers and insurers reroute or pause transit rather than gamble on a vessel getting hit. That risk premium gets embedded directly into crude, and because oil feeds both headline CPI and the transport cost of nearly every other good, a 20%-plus monthly move complicates the Fed's inflation fight at the exact moment it's already debating a hike. Watch the WTI-Brent spread: a widening gap signals traders see the disruption risk concentrated in U.S.-bound Gulf grades rather than the broader global market.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD JUMPS TO 4.74%, ITS HIGHEST SINCE EARLY 2025, AS FED OFFICIALS SAY A HIKE IS NEEDED
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield rose roughly 7 basis points to 4.74% Friday after several Fed officials said publicly they now favor raising rates to get ahead of inflation, two days after the committee held rates steady in a 9-3 vote with three dissents favoring a hike; futures markets are pricing more than a 70% chance of a 25-basis-point hike in September, up from roughly 50% a week ago.
stories.explain: This is the bond market repricing the Fed's path through both the expected-rate and term-premium channels at once: rising hike odds lift near-term yields as investors demand compensation for holding fixed-rate debt into a higher-rate world, and that repricing propagates out to the 10-year as the whole curve adjusts. Officials saying this out loud right after a contested hold is a more forward-looking signal than the vote itself, which is why markets moved on it immediately. With oil now driving inflation expectations higher at the same time, the Fed faces a classic supply-shock dilemma: hiking to fight energy-driven inflation risks slowing growth further, since raising the fed funds rate does nothing to add oil supply.

stories.headline: S&P 500 CLOSES A VOLATILE JULY WITH A 0.7% GAIN AS AMAZON'S RECORD QUARTER OFFSETS A DECLINE IN APPLE
stories.body: Amazon reported revenue of $200.6 billion, up nearly 20% year-over-year, with AWS growing to $42.2 billion at a 39.4% operating margin, while Apple posted its strongest June quarter ever at $109.4 billion in revenue but still fell 1.4% to $333.43 after investors flagged that roughly $0.11 of the EPS beat came from one-time tariff refunds rather than core growth; the S&P 500 added 0.7% to close near 7,490 and the Nasdaq 100 rose about 1% to roughly 28,390.
stories.explain: Wall Street is pricing the quality of earnings, not just the headline beat: AWS's 39% operating margin shows Amazon converting cloud revenue into free cash flow at a rate that funds its own AI capex without diluting shareholders, the same self-funding-growth story that moved Microsoft's stock earlier this week, while Apple's tariff-refund boost is a non-recurring item that mechanically won't repeat next quarter, making the underlying growth rate thinner than the headline number suggests. This is the second earnings pair this week where similar-sized beats produced opposite stock reactions purely on capital-allocation credibility. Because a handful of mega-caps carry outsized index weight, one name's quality miss can offset even a genuinely strong beat like Amazon's at the index level.

stories.headline: GOLD SLIPS TO ROUGHLY $4,086 AS A FIRMER DOLLAR OFFSETS SAFE-HAVEN DEMAND FROM THE HORMUZ ESCALATION
stories.body: Gold eased about 0.3% to roughly $4,086 an ounce even as tensions in the Strait of Hormuz escalated, as the dollar index climbed to 100.12 on rising rate-hike odds and offset the haven bid; the metal remains up more than 2% for July and on pace for its first monthly gain in five months.
stories.explain: Gold is caught between two forces pulling in opposite directions today: rising Fed-hike odds and a firmer dollar raise the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset and make it pricier for foreign buyers, while the Hormuz escalation is exactly the kind of geopolitical shock that normally pushes haven demand higher regardless of rates. When those forces roughly offset, as they did today, the net move tells you which one is dominating at the margin - here, the rates and dollar channel won out. It's a reminder that gold rarely trades on one clean catalyst; a sudden worsening of the Hormuz standoff, like an actual tanker sinking, could flip that balance quickly.

stories.headline: COLORADO AND TENNESSEE JUDGES GRANT A FIFTH SEASON OF ELIGIBILITY TO 30 MORE BASKETBALL PLAYERS, GUTTING THE NCAA'S 'FIVE-FOR-FIVE' RULE
stories.body: U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney in Colorado and a Tennessee counterpart issued preliminary injunctions granting a fifth season to 30 players from the high school class of 2022, including former Michigan State forward Jaxon Kohler and guard Tre Holloman, after finding the NCAA applied its age-based eligibility rules inconsistently across similarly situated athletes; NCAA president Charlie Baker responded by renewing his push for Congress to pass the Save College Sports Act.

stories.headline: LEBRON JAMES SIGNS A TWO-YEAR, $8 MILLION DEAL WITH THE 76ERS, CALLING IT HIS 'LAST DECISION'
stories.body: LeBron James joined Philadelphia on a two-year, $8 million contract, teaming with Joel Embiid and fellow Finals MVP addition Jaylen Brown as the Sixers reload around a 41-year-old James, who said he strongly considered retirement before choosing one more shot at a title; the move caps a wild NBA offseason that has already sent Giannis Antetokounmpo to Miami, Kawhi Leonard to Toronto and Ja Morant to Portland.

stories.headline: EAGLES MAKE JALEN CARTER THE NFL'S HIGHEST-PAID DEFENSIVE TACKLE WITH A FOUR-YEAR, $152 MILLION EXTENSION
stories.body: Philadelphia signed defensive tackle Jalen Carter to a four-year extension worth up to $160 million with escalators and $106 million guaranteed, running through the 2031 season and built around option bonuses and void years that let the team spread cap charges over several seasons; the deal lands as all 32 teams kick off Training Camp: Back Together Weekend and comes days after Deebo Samuel's return to San Francisco and Baker Mayfield's public frustration over Tampa Bay declining to extend him.

stories.headline: ESPN'S PRESEASON TOP 25 PUTS OHIO STATE AT NO. 1, WITH ARCH MANNING'S TEXAS AND HEISMAN HOPES ON THE RISE
stories.body: ESPN's preseason poll opens the 2026 season with Ohio State, Texas, Notre Dame, Georgia and Alabama in its top five, while reigning national champion Indiana - which finished 16-0 as the unanimous No. 1 last season - slots lower as the Big Ten and SEC dominate the board ahead of the 12-team Playoff's third year; Texas quarterback Arch Manning enters as a preseason Heisman favorite, with the AP's official preseason Top 25 set for release Aug. 17.

sports.detail: Washington opens fall camp Aug. 6 with an offensive line returning four starters. Seven Huskies defensive and special-teams players made the East-West Shrine Bowl summer watchlist, and lineman Landen Hatchett was nominated for the AFCA Good Works Team. The Huskies open the season Sept. 5 at home against Washington State in the Apple Cup.

Washington added Rutgers transfer Harun Zrno, a 6-foot-7 Bosnian guard, filling out Danny Sprinkle's roster at 15 for his third season. The staff also hired assistant coach Charles Klask, who brings 25 years of NBA experience, as the Huskies replace departed leading scorers Hannes Steinbach and Zoom Diallo.

Seattle wrapped a chippy Day 6 of training camp Friday, its first practice in pads, with Leonard Williams in the middle of the physicality. The Seahawks signed first-round pick Jadarian Price to complete their 2026 draft class and traded for receiver/special-teamer Irvin Charles from the Jets. Seattle headlines Hard Knocks: Training Camp starting Aug. 11.

The Jalen Duren restricted free agency standoff remains unresolved, with Shams Charania reporting talks could stretch deep into August and the start of training camp emerging as the first real pressure point. Duren, coming off an All-Star, third-team All-NBA year, is seeking a five-year deal north of $287 million and is reportedly weighing his one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer as a fallback.

The Twins rallied past the Mariners 5-3 Friday at T-Mobile Park as Royce Lewis tied it with a seventh-inning homer and Luke Keaschall added a go-ahead double. Seattle and Minnesota play again Saturday and close the series Sunday before the Mariners host Detroit Aug. 4-6.

watchlist: 10-year yield at 4.74% after Fed officials signaled a September hike — CME FedWatch odds above 70%, next major inflation print will be pivotal
Strait of Hormuz tensions — watch for further IRGC action against tankers and any U.S. military response
Jalen Duren restricted free agency standoff with the Pistons — Charania reports talks could stretch deep into August, with training camp as the first pressure point
Washington Huskies open the season Sept. 5 at home vs. Washington State in the Apple Cup
Mariners-Twins series finale Sunday at T-Mobile Park, ahead of a three-game set against Detroit starting Aug. 4

deepDive.title: Option Bonuses and Void Years: The Accounting Trick Behind Jalen Carter's $152 Million Extension
content: Buried inside today's Jalen Carter story is a mechanism that matters more than the $152 million headline: the deal is built around option bonuses and void years, structuring tools that let the Eagles spread a massive cap charge across several seasons instead of absorbing it all at once. The same trick shows up throughout the NFL, and understanding it explains why teams that look 'cap-strapped' on paper can still hand out record-breaking contracts, and why some of those same teams face sudden reckonings years later when the bill comes due.

Unlike real corporate debt, an NFL contract's guaranteed money is typically paid out as a signing bonus, but for salary-cap purposes it isn't expensed in year one - it's prorated evenly across the life of the deal, up to five years, the same way a company depreciates a capital purchase instead of expensing it immediately. An 'option bonus' works identically: it converts what would otherwise be a lump-sum payment into another prorated charge, effectively refinancing next year's cap hit into a smaller slice spread over more years. 'Void years' are seasons tacked onto the back of a contract with no real intention of the player playing them; their only job is to give the proration schedule more years to spread the charge across, after which the remaining balance accelerates onto the cap all at once the moment the deal voids.

What most fans miss is that this is functionally identical to how a company manages debt maturities or amortizes goodwill to smooth reported earnings - it doesn't make the total obligation smaller, it just moves when the expense hits the books. The tradeoff is a future cliff: when a void-year contract ends early or a player is cut, every remaining prorated dollar hits the cap immediately as 'dead money,' which is exactly the mechanism that produced some of the NFL's most infamous cap disasters, like the Broncos absorbing over $85 million in dead money after benching Russell Wilson. Carter's deal avoids that risk today only because the Eagles are confident enough in his long-term value to bet the future accounting will sort itself out.

That same logic - borrowing flexibility today against a promise to true it up later - is exactly what the bond market is pricing into the 10-year yield's move to 4.74% elsewhere in this brief: both are bets that near-term flexibility is worth a defined, deferred cost. For a finance student, the NFL cap is a useful sandbox because the balance sheet is public and the constraint is hard, which makes it a cleaner illustration of deferred-cost structuring than most real corporate filings, where the same proration logic is buried in footnotes rather than laid out play-by-play.
